classifications.label: Instrument resolution exceeds environmental noise: pendulum period genuinely varies at ~0.01 beat precision due to unmeasured environmental factors (air currents, thermal drift, magnetic field fluctuations) or inherent physical variability; no malfeasance, but baseline may be sampling real micro-variation rather than a stable constant.

Instrument calibration baseline is invalid: the pendulum or timing mechanism itself is in a state of continuous micro-drift or micro-oscillation (e.g., pivot wear-in, thermal transient, magnetic coupling to environment) that will stabilize after Day 10, making the current baseline unreliable for post-baseline drift detection.

Procedural error: each reading is being independently recorded with slight variations in timing, temperature logging, or other uncontrolled metadata (e.g., time of day, ambient humidity) that correlate with the beat-count result, creating apparent randomness.

Unknown systematic effect: the event IDs (ranging from ~60 million to ~1.9 billion) encode temporal or environmental metadata that correlates with beat-count in a way not yet recognized; baseline is being confounded by an unmeasured variable.
Post-baseline environment is genuinely noisier or the pendulum has entered a new regime; baseline remains valid but post-baseline scatter reflects real physical change.

Baseline calibration period was too short and pendulum/timing mechanism is still in thermal or mechanical transient; baseline distribution does not represent true equilibrium and post-baseline scatter reflects settling, not environmental change.
Measurement protocol or environmental metadata varies systematically by day or observer, creating apparent scatter that correlates with procedural factors not yet recognized.
Instrument resolution genuinely exceeds noise floor and all 145 readings are physically correct; no anomaly exists, only mismatched expectation.
Event IDs encode hidden temporal or environmental state that correlates with beat count; an unmeasured variable confounds baseline and post-baseline.
Pendulum or timing mechanism is undergoing slow thermal or mechanical drift; baseline is valid but post-baseline readings capture real secular change in the system's equilibrium.

Baseline period (days 1–10) was too short to capture true equilibrium; both baseline and early post-baseline (trials 121–145) reflect active transient, and trials 179–203 reflect later-stage settling; baseline is invalid as a reference.

Environmental conditions (temperature, air currents, pressure) changed between baseline and post-baseline periods, increasing effective noise floor; baseline is valid but post-baseline scatter reflects genuine environmental change, not instrument drift.
Measurement protocol drifted subtly (time-of-day sampling changed, environmental sensor calibration changed, or observer changed); trials 179–203 reflect procedural confound, not physical change.

All readings are physically correct and well-separated; no anomaly exists. The post-baseline scatter and marginal z-score drift are consistent with random environmental noise around a stable mean; expectation of lower scatter was unfounded.

Event IDs encode temporal or environmental state (elapsed time, ambient pressure, magnetic field, or thermal history) that causally drives beat-count variation; a hidden confound correlates with trials 179–203.

Instrument underwent a discrete physical transition (pivot stiffening, thermal lag resolution, or oil redistribution) between trials 295 and 296; bimodal pattern reflects passage through two mechanical equilibria.

Baseline period (days 1–10, n=72) was too short to capture true mechanical equilibrium; trials 1–315 are all still in active transient, and the bimodal pattern in 291–315 reflects nonmonotonic settling, not anomaly.

Environmental conditions changed discretely on day 35 afternoon (trials 296 onward): HVAC schedule, neighboring activity, or external thermal/pressure front caused sustained increase in noise floor and mean shift in trials 296–303, then conditions stabilized by day 36 afternoon (trials 304–315).

Procedural or protocol drift occurred on day 35 (trials 296 onward): time-of-day sampling shifted, measurement technique changed, observer changed, or sensor recalibration was performed; bimodal pattern reflects procedural confound, not physical change.
All readings are physically sound and well-separated; the bimodal appearance is a statistical artifact of small sample size within a day; no underlying anomaly exists, and the instrument is stable.
Instrument underwent discrete mechanical transition (pivot friction change, thermal redistribution, or lubricant state shift) on day 39

Baseline period (days 1–10) was too short to capture true mechanical equilibrium; entire dataset (days 1–40) remains in complex transient, and day 39 shift reflects continuation of settling, not anomaly
Environmental conditions changed on day 39 (external thermal front, HVAC event, or neighboring lab activity); day-39–40 scatter reflects environmental disturbance, not instrument drift
Procedural or observer protocol changed around day 39 (time-of-day sampling shift, timing sensor recalibration, or observer substitution); apparent level change is methodological, not physical
All readings are physically sound and instrument is stable; day-39 level change is a statistical fluctuation in an otherwise stationary process
